title: Piano Concerto No. 20 in D minor
hook: Mozart’s first piano concerto in a minor key, dark and stormy, and the one Beethoven kept playing.

painting.title: The Nightmare
painting.pairingNote: Painted in 1781, the year Mozart settled in Vienna: the dark, uncanny taste of the age, which Mozart’s first minor-key piano concerto brought into the concert hall.

facts: Mozart wrote the concerto in early 1785 for his own concerts in Vienna and played it for the first time on 11 February 1785 in the concert hall of the Mehlgrube, a building on the Neuer Markt.

His father Leopold, who had just arrived on a visit, wrote that the copyist was still at work on the parts when he got there, and that Wolfgang had no time to play the [[rondo|rondo]] through before the concert.

It is the first of Mozart’s two piano concertos in a minor key; the other is No. 24 in C minor. Some of his darkest music is in D minor: the Queen of the Night’s vengeance aria in *The Magic Flute*, parts of *Don Giovanni*, the *Requiem*.
The young Beethoven admired it and kept it in his repertoire. Mozart’s own cadenzas are lost; Beethoven’s are the ones most often played, and Brahms and Clara Schumann wrote cadenzas too.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a storm that gathers in the dark (I), a tender song broken by a sudden squall (II), a fierce chase that breaks into D major at the very end (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: The concerto opens not with a tune but with a murmur: low strings, uneasy off-beat rhythms, a growl in the basses. The storm breaks with the full orchestra, trumpets and drums. When the piano finally enters, it does not repeat the orchestra’s music but brings a lonely theme of its own. The movement is a [[double-exposition|double exposition]] [[sonata-form|sonata form]] and ends quietly.

mainIdeas.name: The murmur
mainIdeas.description: violins and violas restless on off-beat notes, with a short rising growl in the cellos and basses.

mainIdeas.name: The woodwind theme
mainIdeas.description: a plaintive phrase passed between oboe, flute and bassoon.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s theme
mainIdeas.description: a new, singing melody that only the piano plays, heard first when it enters.

stops.hear: Very quiet and uneasy: the upper strings pulse off the beat, and the basses answer with a short, rising growl
stops.happening: No tune yet, only atmosphere; the off-beat pulse is a [[syncopation|syncopation]]

stops.hear: The full orchestra breaks in, loud, with trumpets and drums
The woodwinds alone trade a gentle, plaintive phrase; the orchestra soon overwhelms it
stops.happening: The second theme of the orchestra’s [[exposition|exposition]]

stops.hear: The piano enters alone with a lonely, singing melody nobody has played before
stops.happening: The piano’s own theme: the second exposition begins

stops.hear: The music brightens; piano and woodwinds pass a gentler tune between them
stops.happening: The second theme, in F major

stops.hear: The piano’s lonely theme returns in a new key, then piano and orchestra trade stormy outbursts
The murmuring opening returns in D minor, now with the piano joining in
The orchestra stops on a held chord; the piano plays alone

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The orchestra alone, the drums rumbling; the music sinks to a very quiet close

notice: Notice that the piano never plays the murmuring opening on its own. Its first entry is a different melody, as if it were a character stepping onto a stage.
The movement ends very softly, after all its storms.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Clara Haskil and Igor Markevitch recorded the concerto in Paris in November 1960, with Concerto No. 24; Haskil died in Brussels on 7 December 1960, less than three weeks later. She plays her own cadenzas. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 1–3, followed by Concerto No. 24.

movements.heading: Romance
movements.summary: After the storm, a simple song in B-flat major. The piano sings it alone and the orchestra answers. It is a [[rondo|rondo]]: the song keeps returning, with two different episodes between. The second is a sudden storm in G minor. The trumpets and drums are silent throughout.

mainIdeas.name: The romance
mainIdeas.description: a plain, tender tune, first played by the piano with no accompaniment.

mainIdeas.name: The storm
mainIdeas.description: fast, rushing notes in the piano in G minor, with urgent chords in the orchestra.

stops.hear: The piano alone plays a simple, tender tune
The orchestra answers with the same tune
stops.happening: The tune shared between soloist and orchestra

stops.hear: The piano spins a new, more decorated melody over a soft accompaniment
The simple tune again, the piano alone
A sudden squall: the piano rushes in fast, agitated notes in the minor, the woodwinds answer anxiously
stops.happening: The second episode (C), in G minor

stops.hear: The storm passes and the tender tune comes back

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Quiet closing phrases; the piano ends with a light, rising spread chord

notice: The storm in the middle arrives without warning. Listen to how calmly the song returns afterwards, as if nothing had happened.

movements.heading: Rondo: Allegro assai
movements.summary: The piano shoots upwards from the bottom of the keyboard and the orchestra answers in fury. This rondo races through the minor, with a cheerful tune in F major as relief. After the cadenza the music finally turns to D major, and the concerto ends in brightness, not darkness.

mainIdeas.name: The rocket
mainIdeas.description: a fast rising line in the piano, up the notes of the D minor chord.

mainIdeas.name: The dark second tune
mainIdeas.description: restless and anxious, in the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The cheerful tune
mainIdeas.description: a light, bright melody in F major, first in the orchestra; it returns at the end in D major.

stops.hear: The piano alone races up from low to high, then falls back
The orchestra bursts in, loud and furious
The piano plays a second, restless tune, still dark
Suddenly lighter: a cheerful tune in the orchestra, rounded off by the piano
stops.happening: The third theme, in F major

stops.hear: The piano’s rising rocket again
stops.happening: The rondo theme returns, then wanders through new keys

stops.hear: The orchestra pauses; the piano plays alone
The cheerful tune returns in the woodwinds, now in D major; horns and trumpets brighten the sound

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Loud, bright closing chords
stops.happening: The concerto ends in the major

notice: Listen for the moment after the cadenza when the minor gives way to major. The cheerful tune that offered brief relief earlier now takes over.

threads.title: Darkness and light
threads.body: The concerto moves from the murmuring D minor of the opening to the D major of the last minute; the slow movement is a moment of calm between.

threads.title: A dramatic voice
threads.body: The piano behaves like a character in an opera. It enters with its own tune and never plays the orchestra’s opening alone.

threads.title: Rockets
threads.body: The first movement’s basses growl upwards and the finale’s piano shoots upwards on the notes of the D minor chord; both are rising gestures from the same dark key.
